questions.q: Two files share the same inode number and show a link count of 2. What does this tell you?
options: They are two separate copies of the same original content
They are hard links — two names pointing at the exact same data on disk
One of the files is corrupted
They are symbolic links pointing to each other
questions.explain: A hard link is a second filename pointing at the same underlying data (the same inode). Editing either name edits the same bytes, and the data persists until every linking name is removed.

questions.q: What happens to a symbolic link if the file or directory it points to is moved?
options: The symlink automatically updates to follow the moved target
The symlink keeps a cached copy of the old data
The symlink breaks — it still points at the old path, which no longer resolves to anything
The original file is deleted
questions.explain: A symlink only stores a path string, not the data itself. If the target moves or is deleted, the symlink still points at the old path and becomes a broken link.

questions.q: Why does `tar -cvf backup.tar app/` NOT shrink the total size of the files inside app/?
options: tar always compresses files by default
Plain tar only bundles files into a single archive; it doesn't compress unless you add the -z flag
The -v flag prevents compression
app/ must already be compressed before tar can run
questions.explain: tar (tape archive) combines files and directories into one archive file but applies no compression on its own. The -z flag is what adds gzip compression to the process.

questions.q: What does the `-z` flag do when used with `tar -czf` or `tar -xzf`?
options: Zeroes out the archive's permissions
Adds gzip compression when creating, or tells tar to decompress with gzip when extracting
Zips the files using the .zip format instead of .tar
Deletes the original files after archiving
questions.explain: -z tells tar to pipe the archive through gzip. Used with -c it compresses while creating; used with -x it decompresses while extracting. -f in both cases names the archive file.

questions.q: Why is `zip` considered more self-contained than the `tar` + `gzip` combination?
options: zip cannot handle directories, only single files
zip bundles and compresses files in one built-in format, without needing a separate compression step the way tar does
zip is only available on Windows, never on Linux
zip compresses better than gzip in every case
questions.explain: tar only bundles files and relies on a separate tool like gzip to compress them. The .zip format combines bundling and compression into a single step, which is one reason it's common for cross-platform transfers.
